https://www.politico.eu/article/pope-leo.text: PARIS — Pope Leo XIV urged France to embrace dialogue and diversity Friday, in a veiled swipe at populists as he arrived in Paris for a four-day visit. His appeal came seven months before France’s presidential election, with far-right candidate Marine Le Pen leading opinion polls for the National Rally and traditional parties struggling to hold voters after nearly a decade of Emmanuel Macron’s presidency. “A truly free society” prevents “authoritarian tendencies,” the pope said in a speech delivered alongside President Emmanuel Macron at the Élysée Palace. Advertisement Advertisement The pope named no politician or party. But his defense of diversity and religious freedom lands as Le Pen’s National Rally campaigns against immigration ahead of a presidential election she hopes to win for the first time. “This dialogue is all the more urgent in the context of present-day France, where the people of differing cultural and religious backgrounds are called to live together,” the pontiff continued. Standing in front of French government members and church dignitaries, the pope also argued against pushing religion out of public life, weeks after the National Rally said it was in favor of banning the Muslim headscarf. “Righteous secularism doesn’t mean excluding religion from public spaces,” he said. Macron said the pope brought “hope” to France and praised his work on artificial intelligence and human dignity. The papal visit will take Leo from the Élysée to UNESCO, Notre-Dame Cathedral and a youth vigil at the Stade de France. He will celebrate Mass on Saturday, expected to gather 600,000 people on the Champs-Elysées in Paris. French politics have become deeply polarized in recent years, with the far-right National Rally and the far-left France Unbowed gaining popularity, just as traditional parties struggle to attract voters after a decade of Macron’s presidency. Advertisement Advertisement According to Antonio Spadaro, undersecretary of the Vatican’s Dicastery for Culture and Education, the pontiff will not offer voting instructions while in France nor criticize those who want to vote for Le Pen. Those attracted to nationalism, he said, often have legitimate concerns about identity and “the fear of losing it” but have been “offered the wrong answer.” “The pope will not tell the French to be less French,” said Spadaro in an interview with POLITICO ahead of the visit. “Roots are a good thing. The trouble begins when roots are used as walls.”

Photograph: PR HANDOUT View image in fullscreen The baby, from the Ipswich area west of Brisbane, died almost a week after being taken to hospital with ‘significant internal injuries’. Photograph: PR HANDOUT Queensland Queensland man charged with murder after three-month-old son dies from ‘significant internal injuries’ Uneeb Ullah, 28, from Ipswich, has been remanded in custody after his arrest on Tuesday evening for the alleged murder of the child Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Ben Smee Wed 7 Oct 2026 01.39 EDT Last modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 04.39 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A Queensland man has been charged with the murder of his three-month-old baby son, after the boy died in hospital this week. The infant, from the Ipswich area west of Brisbane, died almost a week after being taken to hospital with “significant internal injuries”. The boy had been on life support. Uneeb Ullah, 28, was arrested on Tuesday evening and charged with the boy’s murder, which is designated a domestic violence offence. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email His matter was mentioned briefly in court on Wednesday but Ullah was not required to appear and did not enter a plea. Police said detectives from the Child Protection Investigation Unit launched an investigation on 1 October after the boy was taken to Ipswich hospital with significant injuries, and that the nature of those injuries prompted hospital staff to report the matter to police. He was later transferred to the Queensland children’s hospital. View image in fullscreen Police arrested Ullah on Tuesday evening. Photograph: PR HANDOUT Speaking to reporters on Wednesday, DI Michael Manago said the mother of the child was “extremely upset” and that both parents, who were born overseas, have limited support. The boy was the couple’s only child. “This is a terribly tragic event involving a very vulnerable young member of the community,” Det Insp. Manago said. “The boy’s mother is extremely upset as you can imagine; this is a terribly tragic event. “She is struggling, but we’re offering her all the support that we can through this very difficult time.” Police said they had spoken to the couple several times since they opened the investigation. The investigation would include looking at the “nature and dynamics” of the boy’s parents’ relationship. “It’s an incredibly confronting and difficult investigation,” Manago said. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion “We were conducting our investigation throughout the last number of days and gathering evidence. When Ullah’s case came before the court on Wednesday, police prosecutor Ben Messina asked it be stood down until later in the day. “I received a phone call this morning … that potentially more material would be provided and asked [that] this matter be stood down to the end of the list,” Messina said of the “relatively vague request”. The magistrate agreed to re-mention the case if other charges were laid. Kirstyn Nicholson, a Legal Aid solicitor representing Ullah, did not apply for bail and sought an adjournment. Ullah was remanded in custody until the matter returns to court on 26 October. – With AAP This story was amended on 7 October 2026. https://www.dw.com/en/hungary-millions-i.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5PRqV Prefer DW on Google Former Hungarian Development Minister Miklos Sesztak is suspected of accepting millions in bribes during Viktor Orban's rule [FILE: July 30, 2017] Image: Robert Szaniszlo/ZUMA/IMAGO Advertisement Hungarian authorities have recovered nearly $20 million (€17.7 million) in hidden cash during a corruption investigation into a former minister under ex-Prime Minister Viktor Orban . The country's newly established National Asset Recovery and Protection Office said Friday that investigators discovered the money during searches linked to former National Development Minister Miklos Sesztak. The discovery is part of a sweeping anti-corruption campaign launched by Prime Minister Peter Magyar, who defeated Orban in April's parliamentary election. Where did Hungarian investigators find the hidden cash? The money was discovered during two days of searches in the capital, Budapest, and three Hungarian counties. Investigators found large quantities of cash buried in forests, concealed in agricultural buildings, warehouses and residential properties, as well as stored in an expensive safe at a secluded location. The recovered money included 5.07 billion Hungarian forints (€13.3 million, $15.3 million), €2.66 million (€2.9 million) and $1.26 million (€1.08 million). According to Finance Minister Andras Karman, 12 employees of the Hungarian State Treasury spent eight hours counting the banknotes using five counting machines. The agency also released a video showing investigators kneeling beside large piles of bundled cash and digging into the ground in what appeared to be a forest at night. Authorities said the seized money had been deposited into an account belonging to the Hungarian state treasury. What corruption allegations does former minister Sesztak face? Sesztak served as Orban's national development minister between 2014 and 2018. He is suspected of accepting more than $37 million (€33 million) in bribes and kickbacks connected to the purchase of overpriced used buses by state-owned transport companies and state construction projects. The former minister was taken into police custody in late September. He has denied wrongdoing. His lawyer, Gabor Papp, so far did not respond to a request for comment on the latest discovery. How has Hungary's Prime Minister Magyar reacted? Magyar described the recovered cash as a turning point in his government's efforts to tackle alleged corruption under Orban. The discovery "officially marks the end of the Fidesz-KDNP mafia," he wrote on Facebook, referring to Orban's former governing coalition. "As of today, Viktor Orbán is a proven mafia boss. A fallen mafia boss. And Fidesz is a criminal organization," Magyar added. Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar has launched a sweeping anti-corruption campaign targeting alleged abuses under his predecessor Viktor Orban [FILE: November 10, 2026] Image: Annegret Hilse/REUTERS Magyar's center-right, pro-European Tisza party won a landslide victory in April, ending Orban's 16-year rule. The new prime minister has pledged to repair Hungary 's relations with the European Union , which had been strained by years of disputes under Orban. His government established the anti-corruption agency with investigative and prosecutorial powers to pursue suspected corruption and misuse of public funds. Who else is being investigated in Hungary's corruption crackdown? Magyar has dubbed the campaign "Operation Purgatory." Several other senior figures from Orban's time in office have been detained as part of separate investigations. Among them is former central bank governor and economy minister Gyorgy Matolcsy, once considered one of Orban's closest allies. Matolcsy is being investigated over the alleged misuse of a central bank foundation that received 288 billion forints ($818 million, €787 million) in public assets. He and other former officials under investigation have denied wrongdoing. Police also detained Orban's younger brother earlier this week as part of an investigation into suspected human trafficking and influence peddling. Viktor Orban's younger brother was detained as part of an investigation into suspected human trafficking and influence peddling [FILE: November 9, 2026] Image: Viktor Veres/HVG/dpa/picture alliance Orban has condemned the investigations as political "tyranny" aimed at removing him from Hungary's political landscape. He has described his brother's detention as an act of political revenge. According to a survey by pollster Median published by news website HVG this week, 70% of respondents considered the anti-corruption campaign "very important." A separate Median survey showed support for Orban's Fidesz party had fallen to 16% of voters by November, roughly half its level before the April election. High-profile figures are being arrested and many Hungarians are pushing for swift accountability, but the rule of law takes time. https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text: Taliban security personnel stand guard at a checkpoint in Jalalabad, Afghanistan, on 2 March. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Taliban security personnel stand guard at a checkpoint in Jalalabad, Afghanistan, on 2 March. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images US immigration Trump ‘whiplash’ on deportations putting Afghans in turmoil: ‘People already survived a war’ Members of Congress and advocates warn that returning people to their home countries could be a death sentence Sanya Mansoor in New York Sat 14 Nov 2026 08.00 EST Last modified on Sat 14 Nov 2026 08.02 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Dozens of Afghans who are currently in the US but fear being deported back to Afghanistan along with a larger group and possibly killed by the Taliban are experiencing “fragile relief” this weekend after it appeared that the Trump administration had put on hold plans to remove them within days. Members of Congress and advocates have repeatedly warned that the deportations could effectively be a death sentence. A flight originally scheduled to transport the group out of the US on election day earlier this month had stayed grounded after a federal judge issued a court order temporarily blocking its departure to Afghanistan or neighboring Pakistan. The whole group numbers more than 150 Afghans, the New York Times reported . And the AP previously reported that the federal government intends to route these detainees to their home country via Pakistan. View image in fullscreen Afghan refugees arrive at a deportation center in Landi Kotal near the Torkham border crossing in Pakistan’s Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province on 28 April. Photograph: Abdul Majeed/AFP/Getty Images Then, as the temporary court order expired last weekend, immigration advocates battling to prevent the deportations talked of dreading that the detainees could be forced to leave the US during the week of 16 November . This prospect was based on a rescheduled removal date given for at least one Afghan man currently in Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention who was due to be on the flight. As that date loomed, suddenly there was another development amid frantic advocacy efforts. Late on Tuesday, it was learned that that detainee, along with a handful of other detained Afghans on the original flight manifest, now no longer had a specified departure date issued by the US government. Some immigration lawyers also reported that their Afghan clients had been moved from staging facilities to long-term detention facilities, suggesting they would not be forced onto a deportation flight in the coming days after all. Amid some confusion and often few details from the administration, Shawn VanDiver, founder and president of the US non-profit coalition #AfghanEvac, said that a sensation of “fragile relief” had descended on the people involved. Some of the Afghans in the targeted group have relatives who assisted the US war on Afghanistan after the terrorist attacks on the US on 11 September 2001 that drove out the Taliban, VanDiver said. He had already called Donald Trump’s efforts to remove Afghans from the US cruel and being done in “a heinous matter” as a scare tactic against others. “In a matter of days, these allies were told they were being sent through Pakistan into the hands of the Taliban, then told they were safe, then told that nobody knows. That isn’t immigration policy. It’s whiplash inflicted on people who already survived a war,” he said. “These men and women kept their promise to America, and it’s time we kept ours by ending these removals for good.” VanDiver has slammed any option to use Pakistan as a conduit for “forced rendition” . Immigration advocates are hoping continued pressure will result in further delays and the ultimate cancellation of that flight and any others planned for the coming weeks. In the meantime, #AfghanEvac is pushing what will become the newly Democratic-controlled Congress in January to pass a bipartisan bill that has been drafted and would give Afghans who are already in the US temporary protected status (TPS) through July 2029, with a vetting process. The US supreme court in June allowed the Trump administration to strip such protections, including from Afghans . View image in fullscreen An Afghan national and her son in the National Conference Center in Leesburg, Virginia, which was redesigned to temporarily house Afghan nationals, on 11 August 2022. Photograph: Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images Such legislation would “keep people we already vetted and brought here from being sent back to the Taliban while their cases are decided”, VanDiver said. Among the passengers reported to be on the blocked flight were Afghans whose relatives helped American troops, women, at least one gay man and members of the minority ethnic Hazara group – some who have said they were previously beaten by the Taliban. Human Rights First, the US-based human rights group, has warned about “ grave, systematic dangers ” for Afghans returned to Afghanistan. That includes “arbitrary detentions, executions, public flogging, and retaliatory violence”, as well as restrictions on basic freedoms for women and girls. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) said in response to questions and a request for comment that the agency complies with all lawful court orders and that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement ( ICE ) does not comment on or confirm prospective removal operations, for operational security reasons, and the safety of its officers. Sari Arvey, director of policy, refugee and immigrant rights at Human Rights First, said that the Trump administration’s targeting of Afghans reflects a broader trend of creating arrangements with other governments to send people back to war zones, security crises and countries that don’t have diplomatic relations with the US. The US suspended relations with Afghanistan after the Taliban government took over in 2021, forcing a scrambled US evacuation. View image in fullscreen Taliban fighters celebrate after the US pulled out of the country, in Kabul on 31 August 2021. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images The Trump administration has held secret talks with Iran about deporting Iranians via a third country, and last Sunday an attorney reported that the US deportation flight of Iranian nationals headed to Iran via Pakistan was abruptly canceled , according to the AP. The Trump administration also is increasingly deporting immigrants to such “third countries”. The supreme court is still litigating in what circumstances the federal government can deport people to regions they have no connection to, though in late September, the court ruled on an emergency basis, allowing Trump to continue this practice . Federal law is designed to prevent the US government from forcing someone to return to a country where they are likely to face torture. The DHS said in a statement that immigrants sent to a third country “receive notice and an opportunity to challenge their removal unless the Department of State is given diplomatic assurances from destination countries” that they would be safe upon return. More than 60 concerned lawmakers in Congress signed a letter to the DHS and the state department, citing relevant law and also calling for the cancellation of any deportation flights of Afghans or Iranians to their home countries, either directly or through any other country. “The United States is also bound not to return anyone to a country where they would face torture, and that obligation does not disappear because a flight makes a stop along the way,” the letter stated. In another letter, New York congressman Gregory Meeks and US senator Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, both Democrats, wrote to Pakistan’s ambassador to the US, urging the Pakistani government not to collaborate in any operation to fly Afghans to Pakistan and then expel them over the border to Afghanistan. The Pakistani embassy did not respond to a request for comment. View image in fullscreen A celebration to mark the fifth anniversary of the Taliban takeover of Afghanistan, in Kabul on 15 August. Photograph: Samiullah Popal/EPA The Afghans targeted are believed to have final removal orders, which means the US can legally deport them. But the fact that an immigrant failed to get asylum or prove to the Trump administration that they have a credible fear about returning to their home country does not mean they don’t face serious risks in their native country, critics argue. The US state department advises Americans: “Do not travel to Afghanistan for any reason,” warning of “civil unrest, crime, terrorism, risk of wrongful detention, kidnapping, natural disasters, and limited health facilities”. The risks for returning Afghans are seen as much greater. “We are talking about people who’ve already been tortured, people who came with evidence – some of the most compelling claims – and the idea that they could find themselves on this flight is pretty horrifying,” said Sarah Mehta, deputy director of immigration policy at the ACLU. “Why would we send Iranians to a war zone or Afghans to one of the most repressive regimes in the world knowing, indeed, that they are going to be targeted because of the very vulnerabilities that led them to flee in the first place?” One Afghan national expected to be on any deportation flight, who has been detained in ICE custody since late 2024, fears returning because his wife is a former member of Afghanistan’s military before the Taliban took over, according to court documents. He is also part of the Hazara Shia group and said he has previously been severely beaten by the Taliban while they searched for his wife. View image in fullscreen Afghan refugees, fleeing the capital Kabul, exit a US Air Force plane upon their arrival at Pristina international airport near Pristina, Kosovo, on 29 August 2021. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images Shaw Drake, assistant professor of law at the University of New Mexico School of Law and co-counsel for the man, said the immigration judge’s not being swayed by these risk factors was “absolutely absurd”. Drake argues that his client had no notice or opportunity to present a claim of fear of persecution or torture in Pakistan. The man’s mental health deteriorated when he was transferred to detention in El Paso, Texas, so much so that a federal court in New Mexico issued a stay for 14 days to ensure the government had enacted safeguards to protect him from the risk of suicide. Another Afghan who could be put on a flight is a Hazara man who testified to immigration officials that he worried about being killed by the Taliban because he reported them to the police when they killed his father, according to US government documents. He said that a few years ago, he was captured, detained, tortured and threatened with death by the Taliban, whose members electrocuted him and beat him with sticks. US federal asylum officers acknowledged the detainee’s testimony but concluded there was insufficient evidence to show the Taliban would inflict severe mental or physical harm towards him if he were sent back. Madhavi Narayanan, a lawyer at Human Rights First, who represents him, said: “It’s another confirmation that our immigration system is not equipped to help those who are fleeing persecution and genuinely seeking safety.” Explore more on these topics US immigration Afghanistan US domestic policy US foreign policy US politics news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness
